findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `HEAD; malicious-command`, `exec` executes it with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct subprocess cancellation
findings.body: `showBranch` returns the spawned `ChildProcess`, but `exec` makes that process an intermediary shell. Calling `.kill()` therefore targets the shell and may leave its Git child running, unlike the previous direct `execFile` process.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct process cancellation instead of wrapping Git in a shell
findings.body:
`showBranch()` returns the spawned `ChildProcess`, so callers can cancel a long-running `git show` via `.kill()`. With `exec()`, that signal targets the intermediary shell rather than Git; on Unix, terminating the shell does not reliably terminate its child. For a large commit/diff or slow repository, Git can therefore continue consuming CPU and buffering output after cancellation. `execFile()` previously returned the Git process directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. A caller-supplied value such as `HEAD; malicious-command` executes that command with the process’s privileges, whereas `execFile` passed it safely as one Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the Git invocation argumentized to prevent command injection
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell and interpolates `branch` directly. Any caller-controlled value such as `main; arbitrary-command` or `$(arbitrary-command)` executes OS commands with the application’s privileges. Retain `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Retain argument-based spawning to prevent unowned resource-consuming subprocesses
findings.body:
On Unix, a branch value such as `x;yes>/dev/null&`—also valid under Git ref-name rules—is interpreted by the shell and starts an indefinite CPU-consuming background process. The returned `ChildProcess` owns only the shell, so cancellation cannot reliably terminate the spawned workload, enabling persistent resource exhaustion.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
